newsitem.title: USA: Mediators open hearings on American, pilots dispute.
newsitem.headline: Mediators open hearings on American, pilots dispute.

text.p: A presidential emergency board opened five days of hearings Thursday to try to resolve the contract dispute between American Airlines and its pilots and head off a potentially disruptive strike.
The board was set up by President Clinton on Feb. 15, less than a half-hour after five days of non-stop bargaining failed and the pilots briefly went on strike against the nation's No. 2 airline.

Going into the opening board session, American Airlines President Donald Carty said, "We're here in the hope we'll end up with an agreement with the Allied Pilots Association that is satisfactory to both of us."
Union President James Sovich, asked if pilot bargaining positions had changed since the strike, said at a separate meeting with reporters, "There is no change from what they were."

The major issues were pay and whether APA pilots or pilots from another union who earn less would fly the small jets that American, a unit of Fort Worth, Texas-based AMR Corp., intends to buy for its regional carrier, American Eagle.
Clinton's naming of the board precludes a strike for 60 days. The board has 30 days to consider the positions of the two sides and try to fashion an agreement both can accept.
American and the pilots union then have another 30 days to consider the board's non-binding recommendation. If the union rejects it, it is free to strike again.
The union has pledged another strike if a satisfactory agreement is not reached, but Congress could end a walkout by passing legislation that mandates binding arbitration.

Board Chairman Robert Harris told reporters before the opening session that the pilots would present their case first and American would present its case on Friday. He said the pilots and then American would further detail their cases next Monday and Tuesday, with rebuttals scheduled for Wednesday.
Harris said that after considering the pilots and American positions, "we will report to the president on how we think the dispute could be resolved."
Union spokesman Wally Pitts said the pilots remained firm in their aim for an 11 percent pay increase to cover the next four years and the past three years, when they had no pay raises.

The airline said it needed the small regional jets that carry 50-70 passengers and needed them flown by pilots paid less in order to compete with the low-cost commuter services being flown by its rivals.

The Allied Pilots Association's 9,300 members who fly American's big jets earn an average of $120,000 a year, while American Eagle pilots in the cockpits of smaller turboprops, members of the Air Line Pilots Association, earn about half that.

The Allied Pilots Association fears that if lower paid pilots fly the smaller jets, which have ranges of up to 1,000 miles, American may gradually move some of the small jets to longer routes, jeopardising the jobs of the union's members.
